newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan wants Western hostages in Kashmir freed.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan wants Western hostages in Kashmir freed.

text.p: Pakistan on Tuesday called for the immediate release of four Western hostages kidnapped by separatist guerrillas in Indian-ruled Kashmir since 1995.
Foreign Affairs Minister Sahibzada Yaqoob Khan repeated Pakistan's demand at a news conference in Islamabad on the eve of a national day of solidarity with Kashmiris.
All government offices will be closed on Wednesday to demonstrate support for Kashmiri militants fighting Indian rule over two-thirds of their Himalayan region.
Pakistan rules the remaining third of the region, over which the two countries have fought two of their three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.

"Let me take this opportunity to repeat our fervent appeal to those involved in the kidnapping of the four Western hostages to release them immediately so that they can join their families," Khan said.
"This reprehensible action is only damaging the cause of the Kashmiri people," he said.
Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells, American Donald Hutchings and German Dirk Hasert were kidnapped by the shady Al-Faran group in July 1995.

Two other men were taken hostage at the time. John Childs, an American, was allowed to escape after a couple of days because he had a bad leg and became a burden to his captors. Norwegian Hans Christian Ostro was found killed in August 1995.

Pakistan denies Indian charges of training and arming the Kashmiri militants, but Khan said Pakistan would "continue to extend all moral, political and diplomatic support to their struggle against Indian occupation".

New Delhi regards the whole of Kashmir as an integral part of India, while Islamabad says the predominantly Moslem Kashmiris must decide in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
Some militant groups seek independence while others want to join Pakistan, which rejects the idea of independence.
Police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence in the Himalayan region since the separatist revolt began.
